newsitem.title: USA: Walter gets grip on AT&T, but future tough.
newsitem.headline: Walter gets grip on AT&T, but future tough.

text.p: AT&T Corp's Chief Operating Officer John Walter is getting high marks from analysts for tackling AT&T's deep-seated problems, but they still see years of struggle ahead.
"I think he's doing a great job of recognizing reality and getting the organization prepared for the future," said Merrill Lynch analyst Daniel Reingold.
Analysts see Walter as a shirt-sleeves manager, a team player more committed to openness than the aloof Chairman and Chief Executive Robert Allen.

"It increases the chance that AT&T will meet its target," said Bill Deatherage an analyst at Bear Stearns. "It is a question of accountability, because it will be clear who delivers and who doesn't," Deatherage said.

Analysts worry about the extent of spending needed for AT&T to enter new local calling markets and expand in wireless while defending itself from an array of tough rivals in the long distance business.
AT&T on Monday said 1997 earnings would be well below expectations because of the cost of new market investments. The company expects to spend $8-9 billion in 1997, compared with $6 billion in 1996.
AT&T said that it expected to reach earnings per share of $5-6 in 2001, compared with $3.47 in 1996. However, analysts say this is a tough target.
"The five year forecast is a stretch. Investors are going to view this as a wait-and-see situation," said Reingold.
AT&T's stock fell 7.5 percent on Monday. On Tuesday, the stock opened 1/2 lower at $36-3/8.
"If all the plans are executed superbly the stock will eventually make a comeback," Reingold said.

AT&T is planning to cut costs by $2.6 billon in the next two years. However, some analysts wondered if this could be achieved without upping the job cuts total from the 11,200 planned over the next two years.
"You can't promise $2.6 billion without lots of extra job cuts," said one analyst who declined to be identified.
Walter's team laid out detailed plans for winning back and holding customers by focusing sales efforts on customer needs rather than product types and by speeding up reaction to marketplace changes.
Walter is expected to take over from Allen as chief executive in 1998 and has enjoyed the full support of AT&T's management so far.
"We brought John Walter in to drive that change to execution of strategy," Chairman Robert Allen said. "I now sense a renewed enthusiasm (within AT&T)," Allen said.
However, analysts scanning the market horizon see heavily armed regional Bells, small aggressive newcomers and traditional rivals like MCI Communications Corp, all hungry for AT&T's customers.
"John Walter's actions are of a leader that people want to follow, but we need to know where we are going," said David Goodtree, an analyst at Forrester Research.
